title: Five Pillars of Good Writing
blocks: What qualities good writing should have · How IELTS Writing is marked

Before taking IELTS, almost everyone has one question in mind: "My English is fairly good, so why do I have so much trouble with IELTS writing?" The answer is very simple. IELTS is not actually a different kind of writing — it is ordinary good English writing with a specific format placed on top of it. In other words, there are two jobs:
First, learn to write correct, clear English.
Then, learn the specific mould (format) of Task 1 and Task 2.

This chapter is about the first job. The funny thing is, we have taken English exams all our lives and memorised essays, but nobody ever told us clearly "what good writing must contain". As a result, even many university graduates cannot answer this question. The points below will help you not only in IELTS but everywhere — job emails, reports, applications.
Good writing has five qualities. Let us look at them one by one.
1. Correctness — writing must be free of mistakes

Small slips, such as teh / recieve, are called "slips of the pen". If there are not too many, they do little harm. But a spelling mistake that changes the meaning of the word is treated by the examiner as "using the wrong word" — this is far more serious:
advice = a suggestion (noun); advise = to give a suggestion (verb)
lose = to misplace / fail to keep; loose = not tight
then = after that; than = used in comparisons
affect = to have an influence on (verb); effect = influence / result (noun)
test = an exam / check; taste = flavour
Make a list of the 10 words you yourself misspell again and again. In the last 2–3 minutes of the exam, look for just those.
All grammatical mistakes are bad, but there are five types of mistake that immediately tell the examiner the writer's foundation is weak. These are all grammar from the lower classes of school:
Yesterday I go to the market.
Yesterday I went to the market.
The number of cars have increased.
The number of cars has increased.
Teachers and parents think they are lazy. (Who is lazy?)
Teachers and parents think students are lazy.
Fix these five before thinking about "advanced" grammar. A student who writes 15 simple but correct sentences will get a higher band than one who writes 10 complex sentences with 6 mistakes.
2. Vocabulary / Lexical resource — range of words
Whether your writing is good can be seen from the words you use. The examiner looks at your range of vocabulary — how many different words you can use correctly. Two rules:
Rule A: accurate, slightly uncommon words instead of common ones — if you are sure
Most students recycle the same 200 common words in every essay. If you can put a more precise word in place of a common one, and you are sure it is correct, then use it:
Students remember essays and write them in the exam. → Students memorise essays and reproduce them in the exam.
a big problem → a serious / major / significant problem
But be careful: using an uncommon word wrongly loses more marks than using a common word correctly. Do not use a word in the exam that you have never seen inside a sentence.
Rule B: not the same word again and again — use synonyms
Suppose the question is: Why do you want to study in a foreign country? Someone wrote:

I want to study in a foreign country because foreign universities are better than universities in my country. Foreign universities have better teachers. If I study in a foreign country I can get a part-time job.
The writing is not wrong, but "foreign" appears four times and "universities" three times — it feels monotonous to read, and the examiner assumes the writer's vocabulary is small. Now the same idea:

I want to study abroad because overseas institutions offer higher standards than those at home. Their teachers are better qualified, and studying in another country would also allow me to work part-time.
The same meaning, but foreign → abroad → overseas → in another country; universities → institutions → those. This is the easiest way to raise your vocabulary score.

Before you start writing, look at the key nouns in the question and write two synonyms for each on the question paper. For example: children → young people, minors, the young; technology → digital tools, devices, innovation.
3. Sentence structure — how sentences are built
Many people think good writing means every sentence is long and complex. That is only half true. Good writing has a mix of three kinds of sentence:
Traffic is heavy in the morning.
Two ideas joined with and / but / so / or
Traffic is heavy in the morning, so many people leave early.
Main idea + a dependent part (because, although, which, when, if…)
Although the metro is fast, many people still drive because they dislike crowds.
Rough guide: one complex sentence after every two simple/compound sentences.

**Golden rule:** A correct simple sentence is always better than an incorrect complex sentence. If you are not sure, break the long sentence into two short sentences and join them with a linking word.
A very common mistake — the double connector. In English, only one joining word goes between two clauses:
✗ Although it was raining, but we went out.   ✓ Although it was raining, we went out. / It was raining, but we went out.
✗ Because he was late, so he missed the bus.   ✓ Because he was late, he missed the bus.
✗ Despite of the rain…   ✓ Despite the rain… / In spite of the rain…
4. Using correct form of voice — Active or Passive?
Among students in our country there is a belief that writing in the passive voice makes writing sound "weighty" or "academic". This is a misconception. Compare:
The decision has been supported by my friends. (passive — heavy, roundabout)
My friends have supported the decision. (active — direct, clear)
The new method is believed to be effective by the teachers. (passive)
The teachers believe that the new method is effective. (active — better)
The active voice is the natural choice. It makes writing lively and strong. Use the passive only in the five cases below:
Who did it (the doer) is not important; the action is what matters
Rice is grown across the delta.
My bicycle was stolen last night.
You deliberately want to keep the doer's name hidden
Several complaints have been made about the service.
Describing a process / method (this is exactly what a Task 1 flow chart needs)
The beans are roasted, then ground, and finally packed.
A polite suggestion to someone senior
This report should be checked again before Friday.
Apart from these five, write in the active voice everywhere else.
Coherence is the biggest topic of this chapter, and it is directly one of the IELTS marking criteria (Coherence & Cohesion). To understand it, you first need to understand what a paragraph is.
A paragraph is a group of sentences that discusses one specific idea. An essay is divided into paragraphs so that the reader can see each idea separately and follow it easily.
How long should a paragraph be?
There is no strict rule, but long paragraphs tire the reader. In modern writing, 80–150 words (roughly 5–8 lines) is ideal.
Beyond 200 words, the reader loses the thread.
For special emphasis you can write a one-sentence paragraph (10–15 words) — this is called an emphatic paragraph. Use it very rarely, and never in Task 1.
Two things are needed to be coherent
Relevance: every sentence stays within the same idea.
Order / Organization (the right sequence): the sentences are arranged in a logical flow.
A good paragraph starts with a topic sentence — in one sentence it tells you what the paragraph is about. Every other sentence should support this topic sentence. Read the paragraph below:

City life and village life are very different. In the city, people work long hours in offices. Long hours make people tired. Tired people often argue with their family. Family arguments can lead to divorce. Divorce is increasing in my country.

The first sentence (the topic sentence) says the paragraph will be about the differences between city and village life. But from the second sentence the writing moves to work → tiredness → family quarrels → divorce. Each sentence is connected to the one before it, but the paragraph as a whole has moved away from the topic sentence (drift). This is a failure of relevance — very common, and a very costly mistake in IELTS.
How to check it yourself: cover everything except the topic sentence. Then read each sentence one by one and ask — "Does this support the topic sentence?" If it does not, cut it or move it.

Another trap — a vague topic sentence. "Many people move to cities." — is the paragraph about why they go, what problems arise, or what the benefits are? The reader cannot tell. Make the topic sentence specific: "People move to cities for three main reasons."
Even if every sentence is relevant, a paragraph is not coherent if the order is jumbled. Here is the same paragraph above, rewritten to be relevant and ordered:

City life and village life differ in three important ways. First, work in the city is mostly in offices and factories with fixed hours, whereas village work follows the seasons. Second, city families are usually small and live far from relatives, but village families are large and neighbours are often cousins. Finally, the cost of living is much higher in the city, especially rent, while villagers often own their land and grow their own food.

Notice the pattern: topic sentence → point 1 (city, then village) → point 2 (city, village) → point 3 (city, village). Every sentence supports the topic sentence, and the reader always knows where they are.

title: Cohesion — connective / signpost words
blocks: The paragraph above uses First, Second, Finally, whereas, but, while. These are called connective words, transition signals or signpost words. They tell the reader in advance what kind of sentence comes next: a new point? The opposite view? An example? A result?

Without connectives, writing reads like a list of separate sentences. With connectives, the ideas flow. IELTS gives marks for this directly. Connectives have nine jobs. We will build a paragraph — about "living in a big city" — and show each job.
1. Starting information — beginning the first point
To begin with, a large city offers far more jobs than a small town.
More: First of all, Firstly, In the first place.
2. Adding similar information — adding the same kind of information
In addition, the best schools and hospitals are usually in the city.
More: Moreover, Furthermore, Besides, Also, Similarly, Likewise, What is more.
For instance, all the country's top universities are in the capital.
More: For example, Such as, To illustrate, In particular, Namely, A case in point is.
However, city life also brings serious problems.
More: In contrast, On the other hand, Nevertheless, Whereas, While, Although, Yet, Conversely, Despite this.

⚠️ **On the contrary** does not mean "on the other hand". It means "rather, the opposite is true". It is used only to reject a mistaken idea: He is not lazy; on the contrary, he works twelve hours a day.
In short, the problems of city living cannot be ignored.
More: In brief, Briefly, To put it simply, Overall.
Clearly, Undoubtedly, Certainly, Without doubt, Obviously, Of course
It seems that, Arguably, Apparently, To some extent, It is true that, Fortunately / Unfortunately
Undoubtedly, anyone moving to the capital must accept a lower quality of air.
⚠️ Never write "According to me". Write: In my view / In my opinion / I believe.
Consequently, thousands of people migrate to the capital every year.
More: As a result, Therefore, Thus, Hence, For this reason, As a consequence, This leads to.
At present I am an undergraduate. At the same time, I am learning to code. After that, I plan to do a master's degree.
At present, Currently, Nowadays, At this time
After that, Subsequently, Afterwards, Eventually, Later
In conclusion, city life offers opportunity at a price.
More: To sum up, To conclude, In summary, Overall.
⚠️ Do not use "At last" (it means "finally, after a long wait"). Do not start a conclusion with "Last but not least".
See the difference — the same paragraph twice

Online learning has grown fast. Students can study from anywhere. They can watch a lesson many times. It is cheaper than a classroom course. There are problems. Students feel alone. Many stop before the end. Online learning is useful. It cannot replace a good teacher.

Online learning has grown fast in recent years. To begin with, students can study from anywhere, and moreover they can watch a lesson as many times as they like. In addition, it is far cheaper than a classroom course. However, there are problems. Many students feel isolated, and as a result a large number give up before the end. In short, online learning is useful, but it cannot yet replace a good teacher.
The same sentences, the same ideas — but the second one feels like "writing", while the first is a shopping list.
Overuse: if every sentence starts with a connective, the writing sounds mechanical — the examiner writes "over-use" and you get stuck at band 6. Aim: one every two or three sentences.
Wrong logic: Moreover before an opposing point, or As a result before something that is not a result — the examiner concludes you do not understand the word's meaning.
Punctuation: a connective at the start of a sentence is followed by a comma (However, …). Whereas / while / although join two clauses in the middle of one sentence, with no capital letter in between.
in addition, moreover, furthermore, besides, also, similarly, likewise, as well as, not only … but also, then, too
first(ly), to begin with, initially, second(ly), then, next, after that, subsequently, afterwards, following this, finally
as a result, consequently, therefore, thus, hence, so, for this reason, it follows that, this leads to, eventually, in that case

however, nevertheless, nonetheless, in contrast, on the other hand, whereas, while, although, even though, though, despite / in spite of (+noun), yet, but, conversely, instead of, rather, compared with, on the contrary (with care)
for example, for instance, such as, to illustrate, in particular, namely, just as, one example is, to exemplify
because (of), since, as, due to, owing to, the reason why, in other words, for this reason, leads to
if, unless, whether, provided that, as long as, so that, depending on, in case
clearly, certainly, undoubtedly, obviously, plainly, of course, without doubt
perhaps, probably, arguably, apparently, to some extent, may / might, possibly
is / refers to, means, that is, in other words, consists of
similarly, likewise, in the same way, alternatively, in comparison, compared with
before, after, since, until, meanwhile, at the moment, when, whenever, as soon as, just as, up to, at present
in conclusion, in summary, to sum up, to conclude, in short, in brief, in a nutshell, overall, to recapitulate, lastly / finally
**Remember:** Using connective words is extremely important not only for IELTS but for any English writing. Pick 2–3 words from each row and keep using them until they feel natural.

title: Your writing through the examiner's eyes: marking and bands
blocks: Of the four IELTS modules, two (Reading and Listening) are objective — each question has only one correct answer, and you can work out your band yourself by checking the answer sheet. But Writing and Speaking are subjective — a trained examiner assesses them, and the same piece of writing may get a slightly different band from two examiners.

This creates a problem: if you prepare alone, you cannot see your own mistakes, and you do not know your real band either. In this chapter the examiner's checklist is given in simple language — so that you at least know what they look for. (Even so, you still need feedback from a teacher or the app's AI grader.)

Every Task 1 and Task 2 answer is scored on four separate criteria, each weighted 25%. Their average is the band for that task. Remember: in the final Writing band, Task 2 carries twice the weight of Task 1.
Did you do exactly what the question asked?
Is it organised in clear paragraphs with good linking?
Is the vocabulary wide and accurate, with correct spelling?
A variety of sentence types, mostly error-free?
2, 3 and 4 are the same in both tasks — they were discussed in the first part of this chapter. Only number 1 is different:
Task Achievement (Task 1): report the main features of the visual, give an overview, accurate data, comparisons, 150+ words, no opinion.
Task Response (Task 2): answer every part of the question, a clear position, ideas developed with reasons and examples, 250+ words.
You did part of the task, not all of it; the format was also wrong in places.
There is no clear overview, or if there is one it is very general — not supported with data.
You mentioned some key points, but not enough; instead you wrote more about less important data.
You answered the question only partly; the format was not always right.
You have a position, but it is not always clear; there is no proper conclusion.
There are some ideas, but they are not developed; some parts are irrelevant.
Information is roughly organised, but progression is limited.
You used connectives, but too few, wrongly, or far too many.
For lack of ideas, you repeated the same thing again and again.
Paragraphs were not divided properly, or you did not use paragraphs.
Vocabulary is limited; it gets the job done, but it is not enough.
Frequent spelling mistakes and wrong words; sometimes hard to read.
Mostly simple sentences; attempts at complex sentences are usually wrong.
Many grammar and punctuation mistakes; in places the meaning is hard to understand.
You attempted everything the task asked you to write.
There is an overview, and the information is selected appropriately.
You caught the key points, but the details contain some errors or irrelevant information.
You answered all parts of the question, though some parts better than others.
The position is clear, although the conclusion is unclear.
The main ideas are there, but some are not properly developed.
Information is arranged logically, with clear progression.
You used connectives well, but sometimes mechanically or wrongly.
You used paragraphs, but not always logically.
You used adequate vocabulary; there are attempts at less common words, with some errors.
There are spelling / word errors, but they do not get in the way of understanding.
You used both simple and complex sentences.
There are some grammar and punctuation mistakes, but the meaning is clear.
You did everything that was required.
You clearly showed the main trends and differences.
You covered the key points properly; they could have been developed further.
You answered all parts of the question properly.
A clear position throughout the writing.
Main ideas are well presented and explained; supporting ideas lose focus in places.
All information and ideas are logically organised and progress smoothly.
You used connectives in a range of situations; under/over-use in one or two places.
Paragraphs are good, each with a clear central topic.
A wide range of words, used accurately; less common words used well.
A variety of complex sentences, with correct structure and use.
Very few grammar and punctuation mistakes.
You wrote everything the task required, appropriately.
You presented and explained all the key points well.
All aspects of the task are well covered.
You used relevant, detailed supporting ideas.
All information and ideas are logically arranged.
Paragraphing is sufficient and appropriate; the linking is barely noticeable.
A varied vocabulary, used fluently and accurately.
Uncommon words used skilfully; errors are rare.
A range of sentence structures used skilfully.
Everything in Band 8, with only the rare slip that even an educated native writer makes under time pressure. Completely natural, flawless, and every demand of the task fulfilled.
Read the ladder — where the big jumps are
From "partial" to "all parts"; an overview appears; the position becomes clear
Answer every part of the question; always write an overview in Task 1; state your opinion in the introduction itself in Task 2
From "some errors" to "very few errors"; ideas get developed; linking becomes natural
Cut any sentence you are not sure of; give explanation + example for every idea; fewer but accurate connectives
From "good" to "skilled and precise"; almost no errors
More precise, wider vocabulary; more variety in structure; one full revision pass

**The most common reason for getting stuck at Band 6:** the writing is mostly correct, but the ideas are only listed, not developed; and every paragraph has one or two "clumsy" mistakes. Both can be fixed.
Estimate your own band — a quick self-test
After writing an answer, tick honestly:
I answered every part of the question (T2) / I reported the main features with an overview (T1).
My position is clear in the introduction and conclusion (T2 only).
Every idea has at least one sentence of explanation, and in Task 2 an example.
Only one topic in each paragraph.
One linking word every two or three sentences — not in every sentence.
No linking word is repeated, and none is used with the wrong meaning.
No key noun appears more than twice in one paragraph.
I did not use any word I am unsure of.
I checked my usual spelling mistakes.
At least one correct complex sentence in each paragraph.
I checked subject–verb agreement and tense.
All ticked → probably Band 7 or above. Half ticked → Band 6. Fewer → Band 5. Do this after every practice, before looking at the AI feedback.
